replies:
Yes, absolutely—screening for hepatitis B at your first prenatal visit is strongly recommended and is a standard part of prenatal care in many countries, including the U.S. It’s a simple blood test that checks for the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which indicates current infection.

**Why it’s so important**  
Hepatitis B can be passed from mother to baby during childbirth. Without preventive treatment, up to 90% of infected newborns become chronic carriers and face a higher lifetime risk of liver disease, cirrhosis, or liver cancer. Knowing your status early lets your medical team take steps to protect your baby right after birth.

**What happens if you test positive**  
If the test shows you have hepatitis B, your baby will receive two injections within 12 hours of birth: the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine and a dose of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG). This combination prevents transmission more than 90% of the time when given on time. Your pregnancy may also be monitored a bit more closely, and you might be referred to a liver specialist for your own health.

Even if you were vaccinated against hepatitis B in the past, screening is still recommended because the test looks for active infection, not immunity, and it’s possible (though rare) to have chronic infection despite vaccination.

**The bottom line**  
This screening is safe, quick, and one of the most effective things you can do for your baby’s long-term health. Bring it up with your OB-GYN or midwife at that first visit—they’ll likely already have it on your lab order list, but it never hurts to confirm. Congratulations on your pregnancy—you’re already taking a great step by asking this question!

Yes, I'm very certain—this is one of the most well-established, evidence-backed recommendations in prenatal care. Let me give you more detail on why there's no doubt.

**Official guidelines are unanimous**
- The **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)** gives universal hepatitis B screening in pregnancy its strongest recommendation (Grade A), meaning the evidence of benefit is high.
- The **CDC**, **American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)**, and the **World Health Organization (WHO)** all say the same: every pregnant person should be tested for HBsAg at the first prenatal visit, regardless of vaccination history or risk factors.

**Why it's not something to skip**
- Many people with chronic hepatitis B have no symptoms and don't know they're infected. Risk-based screening (testing only those with known risk factors) misses a large portion of carriers, which is why universal screening is the standard.
- Without knowing your status, you can't get the right protection for your baby. The birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine alone isn't enough if you're HBsAg-positive—the baby also needs HBIG within 12 hours. The timing is critical, and it only works if the team knows in advance.

**What if you've been vaccinated?**
- The vaccine prevents *new* infection; it doesn't treat an existing chronic infection. The screening test (HBsAg) detects the virus itself, not immunity. So even if you were vaccinated years ago, you could still have a chronic infection from before vaccination (or, rarely, a vaccine-escape infection). That's why testing is still done.

**Bottom line**: It's not only "recommended," it's an expected part of routine prenatal labs. If your provider doesn't offer it, they are not following standard care. I'm confident in this because it's a core public health measure that has dramatically reduced mother-to-child transmission in countries that implement it.

I hope that helps put your mind at ease. If you have any concerns about why you're being tested or what the results mean, your prenatal care team will be happy to walk you through it in detail.

DO IT

It's a standard, strongly recommended test that protects your baby from a serious, preventable infection. The benefits are huge, the risks are none, and it's an expected part of routine prenatal care.
